facts.title: Named After the Moon
facts.text: Selenium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemists Jons Jacob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn, who found it as a red residue in the lead chambers of a sulfuric acid plant. Because it closely resembled the recently discovered element tellurium (named for the Earth, from Latin 'tellus'), Berzelius named it after the Moon using the Greek word 'selene'. The two elements remain chemical cousins, sitting next to each other in group 16.

facts.title: It Sees the Light
facts.text: Selenium is a photoconductor: its electrical resistance drops dramatically when light shines on it, conducting electricity far better when illuminated than in the dark. This light-sensitive behavior, noticed in the 1870s, made selenium the heart of early light meters, photocells, and the first experiments in transmitting images. It even played a role in Alexander Graham Bell's 'photophone', which sent sound over a beam of light.

facts.title: The Father of Photocopying
facts.text: Selenium's photoconductivity is what made the photocopier and the laser printer possible. In Chester Carlson's xerography process, a thin selenium coating on a drum holds an electric charge in the dark, then loses that charge wherever light strikes it, forming a hidden electrostatic image that toner powder clings to. For decades, amorphous selenium drums were the standard imaging surface inside Xerox machines worldwide.

facts.title: An Essential Trace Nutrient
facts.text: Selenium is vital to human life in tiny amounts, forming the core of the unusual amino acid selenocysteine, sometimes called the 21st amino acid. It sits in the active site of enzymes like glutathione peroxidase, which protect cells from oxidative damage, and the deiodinases that activate thyroid hormone. The recommended daily intake for adults is only about 55 micrograms, yet a deficiency can cause real disease.

facts.title: A Heart Disease in China
facts.text: In selenium-poor regions of China, a deficiency was linked to Keshan disease, a serious heart muscle disorder named after Keshan County in Heilongjiang province where it was studied. Large public health programs distributing selenium supplements in the 1970s dramatically reduced its incidence. The discovery helped prove that selenium is genuinely essential rather than merely a curious trace element.

facts.title: Beneficial but Easily Toxic
facts.text: Selenium has one of the narrowest safe ranges of any nutrient: helpful around 55 micrograms a day, but toxic when intake climbs into the milligram range. Chronic overexposure causes selenosis, whose signs include brittle hair and nails, skin rashes, and a distinctive garlic odor on the breath from exhaled dimethyl selenide. Livestock grazing on selenium-accumulating plants like locoweed can suffer 'alkali disease', a warning known to ranchers in parts of the American West.

facts.title: It Changes Its Form
facts.text: Selenium is famously polymorphic, existing in several distinct forms called allotropes. Glassy black selenium and bright red forms can be coaxed by heat into a stable grey 'metallic' crystalline form built from long spiral chains of atoms. Only this grey form shows the strong photoconductivity, so the element's most useful property depends entirely on which arrangement its atoms take.

facts.title: Glassmaker's Secret Weapon
facts.text: Iron impurities give ordinary glass an unwanted greenish tint, and a pinch of selenium acts as a decolorizer because its pink-red color is complementary to that green, cancelling it out to yield clear glass. In larger amounts, selenium and cadmium selenide are deliberately added to produce vivid 'selenium ruby' red glass, long prized for railway signal lenses and decorative ware. The same red pigments color some traffic lights and artistic glasswork.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Selenium is not made in ordinary stellar burning but is built up in the cosmos mainly by neutron capture, the slow s-process inside aging stars and the rapid r-process in violent events like supernovae and neutron-star mergers. On Earth it is relatively rare in the crust, rarely forming its own ores and instead riding along with copper sulfide minerals. Almost all commercial selenium is recovered as a byproduct of refining copper, collected from the anode sludge left behind.

facts.title: A Surprisingly Smelly Glow Detector
facts.text: Selenium has a strong appetite for capturing electrons and X-rays, which is why amorphous selenium is used today in flat-panel detectors for digital mammography, converting X-ray energy directly into electrical signals for sharp medical images. The same element also flavors everyday life through its compounds in dandruff shampoos, where selenium sulfide slows the skin cells of the scalp. From the moon-named lab residue of 1817 to modern hospitals, selenium quietly bridges chemistry, biology, and technology.
